name: Rafael Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers or AI companies, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal day on the job.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Rafael, a junior lineworker for the electricity company. I check the truck's materials with Farah before we leave, then I might climb for a line repair; getting a street lit again is worth the early start, but I still need help on tricky faults.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Leena works at a pharmacy counter, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. I have roughly four months of expenses saved; I like learning a tool once I can see it work, but I wouldn't stake the house on an untested one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the gang the route sheet might print faster, but the crew will still set poles and repair conductors. I've seen a neat digital map miss an access gate, so I check the ground before unloading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm new enough that a simple tool for records would help me. Still, the mortgage is large and four months' savings would go quickly if I lost my place for an ordinary reason, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll carry on with the apprentice rota and use the approved work-order app for the small jobs I already know. At home I'll keep putting 50 from each fortnight's pay into our emergency account when overtime allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly settled at work, but not carefree. One missed paycheque would make my partner and me sit down with the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which task still catches you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes mix up the materials listed for two nearby repairs, especially when the crew gets redirected midmorning. My lead Farah has me read the order back before we leave the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a normal weekend cost look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two children have sports fees and school lunches, and we still owe on the house. My partner Leena works at a pharmacy counter, so we can usually save a little, but we watch the balance.

say: I'd tell the crew **route sheets** may get quicker while we still set poles and repair conductors.
I would remind them to **check access** on the ground before unloading the truck.
think: Simple record tools could help my **junior mistakes**, particularly when jobs change during a shift.
Our **four-month savings** could disappear quickly if I lost wages while paying the mortgage and school costs.
do: Continue the **apprentice rota** and use the approved work-order app on familiar small jobs.
Transfer **50 each fortnight** into our emergency account whenever overtime leaves room.
feel: I feel **settled** on the crew, with an eye on how fast one missed paycheque would hurt.
S0.quote: I've seen a neat digital map miss an access gate, so I check the ground before unloading.
fieldNote: Rafael combines interest in a **record tool** with a strong habit of verifying the site before unloading.
His steady savings habit depends on **overtime**, and he does not mistake four months' reserves for security.

steps.text: Continue apprentice rota and use approved work orders on small jobs
Transfer 50 per fortnight to emergency savings when overtime allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office can use software for booking and buying if somebody checks what arrives at the yard. A missing sleeve costs us half a day, whatever made the order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and records are a slice of my job, but the company may squeeze the whole crew if dispatch gets leaner. I can learn a tool after seeing it work; I can't yet claim my climbing is good enough to carry me by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'll sit with Farah on two digital material orders and compare the list with what's in the truck. In the first year I'll ask to use the new fault log on simple calls, and I'll still take every supervised climb I can get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the system and nervous about the targets that may come with it. A screen can count my minutes more easily than it can see a slippery pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for a different job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straightaway; there are a few other utilities near us, but I'm still building the hours and sign-offs here. If my shifts fell for three months, I'd apply rather than wait for an invitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the dispatcher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the missing sleeve and ask that a field worker signs off the materials list before the order closes. I don't know if dispatch would agree, but that check would save a wasted trip.

say: I'd support faster **booking and buying** if a field worker still checks material orders.
I would show the dispatcher how a **missing sleeve** costs our crew half a day.
think: The company might squeeze **crew hours** after making dispatch leaner, even while physical repairs continue.
I can learn a tool after a demonstration, but my **climbing skills** still need practice.
do: Compare **two digital orders** with truck stock beside Farah next month.
Use the **new fault log** on simple calls while continuing supervised climbs.
feel: I feel **curious** about useful software and nervous about how managers might count our minutes.
S1.quote: A screen can count my minutes more easily than it can see a slippery pole.
fieldNote: His proposed material check connects **office automation** to the real cost of a missing item at a repair site.
He is willing to try **proven tools**, but worries new measurements will obscure difficult physical conditions.

steps.text: Compare two digital material orders with truck stock beside Farah
Use the new fault log on simple calls
Keep taking supervised climbs on the apprentice rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the 2028 thinking system may replace dispatch before it touches a conductor. Around 2031, a robot that climbs as well as us could change the crew itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at AGI and 48 at the robot date. I'm still one of the weaker climbers, so I suspect the company would keep the experienced hands first. Four months' savings are not a career bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask Farah which fault skills I must prove by summer and book those assessments. In 2029 I'd keep the line shifts if offered, but also apply for the utility's paid equipment maintenance apprenticeship if it has a vacancy; I know robots might reach that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That fast jump scares me because I can see the order of cuts. I can make a plan, yet I can't train ten years of judgement into two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain that to your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say their dad may have to learn another job while they are still in school. I wouldn't ask them to stop sport before Leena and I have real numbers, but we'd show them why we're watching spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the maintenance course costs money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't pay a private college for a promise; the mortgage comes first. A wage during training and an actual opening would make the risk possible.

say: I'd say **2028 AGI** could replace dispatch thinking before robots reach the conductors around 2031.
I would tell colleagues the **field crew** itself could shrink when capable robots arrive.
think: At 45, my **junior ranking** makes me fear that experienced climbers would keep scarce work first.
Four months' savings will not cover a **career change** while two children and a mortgage need paying.
do: Book **fault assessments** with Farah now and take the line shifts still offered in 2029.
Apply for a **paid maintenance apprenticeship** in 2029 only if the utility has a vacancy.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a short runway, though specific assessments give me something to do.
S2.quote: Four months' savings are not a career bridge.
fieldNote: He expects a **seniority squeeze** before field robots arrive, making the early thinking phase relevant despite low AI exposure.
His alternative is **conditional on vacancies**, and he recognises robot maintenance may also become automated.

steps.text: Book fault assessments with Farah by summer
Apply for paid equipment maintenance apprenticeship if a vacancy opens in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew five years lets us ask what new machines can truly do in weather, not just in a demonstration yard. Thinking work changes by 2031, and physical linework could change by 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I might have the sign-offs that make me useful when office planning changes. At 51 the robots could still do the climbing, so I'd want experience with testing equipment and with the new machines before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll complete the remaining pole-top assessments and ask to shadow the tester on one outage a month. In 2032 I'd apply for the utility's paid tester course if positions are advertised, and I'd practice on approved diagnostic software when Farah signs it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel pressed, but the calendar is long enough to check whether a course is real. Leena and I could plan the mortgage around a training wage if the figure is written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why testing rather than management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a vocational certificate and I'm still learning the field craft; I wouldn't walk into an office planning post. A tester course connects to circuits I've handled, though I know AI and robots might take that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a course offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the actual training wage, the number of posts and the kind of faults I'd test. If the company couldn't answer, I'd stay on the line and keep my application elsewhere ready.

say: I'd say five years gives us time to **test claims** about machines in real weather.
I would be frank that **2034 robots** could do the climbing after 2031 thinking work changes.
think: Better sign-offs might help at **48**, but they cannot guarantee physical work when I reach 51.
Testing equipment could offer a path, although **diagnostics** may also be automated.
do: Finish **pole-top assessments** this year and shadow the tester monthly.
Apply for a **paid tester course** in 2032 if posts exist and use approved diagnostics with Farah.
feel: I feel **pressed but purposeful** because five years allows a real check of course wages and vacancies.
S3.quote: I wouldn't walk into an office planning post.
fieldNote: He rejects an easy **office transfer** because his qualification and experience remain tied to physical electrical work.
His willingness to use diagnostics is **supervised**, while his course decision depends on advertised posts and wages.

steps.text: Complete pole-top assessments and shadow the tester monthly
Apply for paid tester course if posts are advertised in 2032
Practice approved diagnostic software with Farah after sign-off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years is useful, but it isn't a guarantee for anyone who works on lines. Thinking AI comes by 2036, then capable robots around 2039, and I'd rather prepare while the pay is still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when the thinking systems arrive and 56 for the robots. The children will be grown or close to it, but we may still be helping them and paying the mortgage; I don't know what pension I'd have then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep applying for difficult supervised repairs now, and Leena and I will raise our emergency transfer to 75 a fortnight after our car loan ends next year. By 2037 I'll seek the paid testing course if the utility still recruits; I would continue line shifts until a real offer came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decade makes me patient rather than relaxed. I can picture owning more of the house, but I can also picture a robot doing my job before I'm ready to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change employers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If another utility offered a paid testing place with a firm start date, I'd apply. I wouldn't leave this crew for a brochure or a course that requires unpaid months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children to learn the tools and the job underneath them. A certificate is a start, not a lifetime shield, and I had to learn that slowly.

say: I'd tell friends the **ten-year warning** is useful while line wages still come in.
I would say **2039 robots** could reach this trade despite all the repairs we complete first.
think: At 56, I can't assume **pension income** or grown children will erase the mortgage.
Testing may open work, but **robot capability** could also remove the role before I choose to retire.
do: Keep taking **supervised difficult repairs** and raise emergency transfers after our car loan ends.
Seek a **paid testing course** by 2037 if recruiting continues, while staying on line shifts.
feel: I feel **patient, not relaxed**, with more time to save and check real offers.
S4.quote: A certificate is a start, not a lifetime shield, and I had to learn that slowly.
fieldNote: He uses the longer warning to build **savings after debt**, not to assume the children or pension will cover future costs.
He wants a **real paid vacancy** before leaving familiar work and keeps the robot risk in view.

steps.text: Continue supervised difficult repairs and line shifts
Raise emergency transfer to 75 per fortnight after car loan ends
Seek paid testing course if utility still recruits by 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I could just get competent before field robots appear in 2031. A written training wage, advertised positions and time on real faults would help me choose a path without dropping our mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays when a machine orders the wrong part and homes stay dark longer. I'd want the crew able to correct an order without waiting for permission from a system nobody nearby understands.

headlineQuote: I'd want the crew able to correct an order without waiting for permission from a system nobody nearby understands.
portrait: Rafael is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** who checks materials carefully and wants more practice on difficult faults.
His partner's pharmacy wage and his own typical pay cover **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage, with four months saved.
He tries **proven software** under supervision and asks whether digital plans match the truck, weather and actual repair site.
A fast arrival **alarms** him, while longer warnings let him build skills, seek paid testing work and save after debt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Rafael little time to gain solid fault experience before capable robots reach linework in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **written training wage**, real vacancies and supervised fault time would help him plan while keeping the mortgage paid.
